clue.text: Monumental blunders

parts.note: the phrase reads as huge mistakes, but also as costly ornamental towers and fake ruins built on country estates with no practical use

explanation.walkthrough: A folly is both foolishness and an extravagant ornamental building put up purely for show, so these blunders are literally monumental.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornamental structures built for no purpose are called by the same word as acts of foolishness.

clue.text: Exercise warmed up small runner, much smaller than 24

parts.note: fired means heated, as pottery is in a kiln
a rill is a tiny stream, far smaller than the great river at 24

explanation.surface: A training run where someone warms up and then runs a little.
explanation.walkthrough: FIRED (warmed up) + RILL (a little stream, a 'runner' being flowing water, tiny next to London's river at 24).
explanation.definitionFit: A practice evacuation of a building is a safety drill against blazes.

clue.text: Name of the game winner losing height

parts.note: Ludo is a children's board game played with dice and counters

indicators.note: losing means dropping, so the hill is taken out of the champion

parts.note: a victor is one who wins
a tor is a rocky hill, especially on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A request for the champion of the game, who has shrunk.
explanation.walkthrough: LUDO + VICTOR without TOR (a craggy hill in south-west England) leaves VIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludovic is a man's given name, a form of Louis.

clue.text: Site of Yeats's restful cabin …

parts.note: W. B. Yeats's poem about an island in Lough Gill where the speaker will build a small cabin and find peace

explanation.walkthrough: Yeats's poem The Lake Isle of ... opens 'I will arise and go now', planning a small cabin of clay and wattles.
explanation.definitionFit: The lake island in County Sligo is where Yeats's poem places its peaceful hut.

clue.text: … and the rest not long delayed

definitions.meaning: 'and the rest' is 'and ...', so the rest is ...

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words the answer is the 'so on' of 'and so on', meaning 'and the rest'; read as one word it means shortly. The ellipsis just runs on from 3 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two it completes the phrase meaning et cetera; whole, it means presently.

clue.text: To whom windmills were giants

parts.note: points to the deluded Spanish knight of Cervantes's novel, who charged at windmills believing them to be giants

explanation.walkthrough: In Cervantes's novel the hero tilts at windmills, mistaking them for giants.
explanation.definitionFit: Cervantes's knight-errant famously attacked windmills he took for monstrous giants.

clue.text: A prophylactic 40 days

parts.note: the word comes from Italian for forty days, the period ships were held to prevent plague spreading

explanation.walkthrough: Venetian ports held ships for quaranta giorni, forty days, to keep out plague.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolation to prevent infection was originally a forty-day period.

clue.text: It may be gold, or 50 per cent gold and tin

definitions.text: It may be gold, or 50 per cent gold and tin

indicators.note: may be suggests the following letters could form something else, signalling a rearrangement
fifty per cent is half, so only the front half of the second gold is used

explanation.surface: A bar of metal might be pure gold, or an alloy of half gold with tin.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of 'gold' is GO; 'may be' rearranges GO with TIN. 'Or' is heraldic gold, adding to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A cast bar of metal, often precious, is an ingot.

clue.text: Great lake, not, oddly enough, a S American port

indicators.note: oddly suggests something strange, so the letters of not and a are put in an odd order

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian port

explanation.surface: Describing a large lake that, strangely, is not a South American harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges NOT and A to ONTA, then RIO follows. 'Oddly' tempts you to take alternate letters; the counts do not work.
explanation.definitionFit: One of North America's five Great Lakes, between Canada and New York State.

clue.text: Like Omar's final glass

parts.note: FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam ends with the request to turn down a vessel with nothing in it

explanation.walkthrough: The last line of FitzGerald's Rubaiyat is 'Turn down an empty Glass!'
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian poet's closing cup holds nothing, vacant of wine.

clue.text: Admiral drops Marshal in to — see sculptor

indicators.note: drops means lets fall away, so the Marshal's name is removed from the admiral's

parts.note: Admiral George Rodney, eighteenth-century British naval commander
Michel Ney, one of Napoleon's marshals

explanation.surface: A naval commander loses a field marshal and is sent to visit an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove NEY (Napoleon's Marshal Ney) from RODNEY (the British admiral) to leave ROD, then add IN; 'to see' joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Auguste Rodin was the French artist who made The Thinker in bronze.

clue.text: Operating can break a butterfly

indicators.note: breaking the word operating into pieces and reassembling it signals a rearrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A surgical procedure might crush a delicate insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can break' tells you to rearrange the letters of OPERATING.
explanation.definitionFit: The orange-tip is a common European white butterfly, the male marked with bright orange wing tips.

clue.text: Art descending to strip ?

definitions.meaning: in archaic English 'thou art diving' can be put 'thou ...', the -st ending standing for art
to deprive someone of clothing or possessions

explanation.walkthrough: The first definition plays on old second-person verbs: 'thou divest' would mean 'thou art diving', that is, art descending.
explanation.definitionFit: Plunging downward in old thou-form speech, and also to deprive someone of clothes or property.

clue.text: "A wise and —— inactivity" (Mackintosh)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the Scottish historian Sir James Mackintosh, praising Parliament for skilful doing nothing

explanation.walkthrough: Sir James Mackintosh wrote of the Commons remaining 'in a wise and masterly inactivity'; the missing word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective in the quotation means skilful, showing the command of an expert.

clue.text: Make over-nice distinctions with a trichological problem

definitions.meaning: trichology is the study of the scalp, so a hair complaint like divided ends

explanation.definitionFit: To quibble pedantically, and literally hair strands that have split at the ends.

clue.text: Bring upon oneself a runic spell

indicators.note: spell here is a magic charm, which transforms the word runic into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone carved an ancient enchantment and suffered the consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell' is the signal to rearrange RUNIC; 'a' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a debt or penalty is to make yourself liable to it.

clue.text: Mrs Wiggs's needlecraft ?

parts.note: Mrs Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch is an American novel, so her labour is the work of the Patch, which also names quilting from scraps

explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch (Alice Hegan Rice, 1901) lives in the Patch, so her work is literally Patch work.
explanation.definitionFit: Sewing together scraps of fabric into a quilt is a craft named after those pieces.

clue.text: A bit of a knotty problem if the rest have to hike?

definitions.text: A bit of a knotty problem if the rest have to hike?

parts.words: A bit of a knotty problem if the rest have to hike
parts.note: one kind of knot, read also as half of thumbing a lift while the other half walks

explanation.walkthrough: It is a simple knot (a bit of a 'knotty problem'); read as hitch-hiking, half the party gets a lift and the rest must walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple sailors' knot made by passing a rope's end round an object and under itself.

clue.text: Sleeping-bags for soldiers? Sound idea

indicators.note: sound means said aloud, so the idea is a phrase heard rather than read

parts.note: bags for a nap, nap sacks

explanation.surface: Proposing bedrolls for the troops as a sensible plan.
explanation.walkthrough: Bags for napping, NAP SACKS, said aloud give the soldier's packs; 'Sound idea' poses as praise for a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers carry their kit in canvas backpacks.

clue.text: Sordid money tin contains a sort of philosophy

parts.note: filthy lucre is the stock phrase for money gained dishonourably

indicators.note: contains means holds inside, so the tin wraps around the letter a

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A grubby cash box holds a particular school of thought.
explanation.walkthrough: LUCRE (sordid money) followed by TIN with A placed inside it, TIAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet Lucretius set out Epicurean atomism, and that school of thought bears his name.

clue.text: Giving up a sitting, say

indicators.note: say means spoken aloud, signalling a word that sounds like another

parts.note: a session is a sitting of a court or council

explanation.surface: Abandoning a meeting, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' signals that SESSION, a sitting, is heard as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The surrender of territory or rights to another party is a ceding.

clue.text: Morning, all! Back from the Zoo ?

indicators.note: back means read in the opposite direction, turning the greeting's words end to end

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for morning, ante meridiem
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheery greeting to everyone on returning from a day at the zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns AM + ALL around to give the animal; the definition is by example, a creature you might see at the zoo.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American pack animal is a typical zoo resident.

clue.text: Scotsman in real trouble with a hospital worker

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the Scotsman sits within the troubled letters
trouble suggests disorder, so the letters of real are rearranged

parts.note: mon is a Scots form of man, as in 'hoots mon'

explanation.surface: A Scot in serious difficulty alongside a hospital employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' rearranges REAL to ALER, and 'in' puts MON (Scots for man) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Formerly a British hospital social worker who looked after patients' welfare.

clue.text: Jumble, it's cheap imitation

indicators.note: to jumble is to mix up, so the letters of it's cheap are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A muddled mixture dismissed as a poor-quality copy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumble' signals rearranging ITSCHEAP; the word itself also describes the answer, a medley.
explanation.definitionFit: A work deliberately copying the style of another artist or period is a pastiche.

clue.text: Took steps to cover up head journalist

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a cap is a covering or lid
ED is short for editor, head of a newspaper's journalists

explanation.surface: Moves made to conceal the chief reporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns CAP to PAC in this down clue; ED follows. 'to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Walked with measured strides.

clue.text: Press clubs ?

definitions.meaning: to smooth clothes with a heated appliance
golf clubs with angled metal heads

explanation.definitionFit: To smooth laundry flat, and also metal-headed golf clubs.

clue.text: Liquid that some seek to prove inflammable

definitions.text: Liquid that some seek to prove inflammable

parts.words: Liquid that some seek to prove inflammable
parts.note: alludes to the saying about an ambitious person trying to set London's river on fire, that is, to do something remarkable

explanation.walkthrough: To 'set the Thames on fire' is a British idiom for achieving something spectacular; the river is London's.
explanation.definitionFit: London's river is the water in the idiom about making a great stir by setting it ablaze.

clue.text: Star for instance in an American state

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the example abbreviation sits within the state

parts.note: VA is the abbreviation for Virginia
EG, exempli gratia, means for example

explanation.surface: An example of a celebrity in one of the US states.
explanation.walkthrough: EG inside VA (Virginia).
explanation.definitionFit: The brightest star in the constellation Lyra.

clue.text: Dernier cri ? No line for modern fashion, it appears

definitions.text: Dernier cri ? No line for modern fashion, it appears

indicators.note: it appears means the item shows itself within the run of clue words, ignoring spaces and punctuation

explanation.surface: Once the latest cry of fashion, the hooped skirt has no place in today's styles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it appears' points to the letters running through 'cri ? No line'. The hooped petticoat was once the dernier cri, French for the very latest fashion, but has no line in modern dress.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiff hooped petticoat worn under Victorian skirts was once the height of fashion but is long outmoded.

clue.text: Note what the doctor ordered

definitions.meaning: in music the keynote, first degree of a scale
a restorative medicine, and by idiom something exactly needed

explanation.definitionFit: The keynote of a musical scale, and a pick-me-up medicine a physician might prescribe.

clue.text: Hardy, power-house men

definitions.meaning: Thomas Hardy's epic verse drama about the Napoleonic wars has this title
rulers of powerful houses or families

explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy's verse drama on Napoleon carries this title, and hereditary rulers of mighty families bear the word.

clue.text: Sticks terribly hard, see ?

indicators.note: terribly suggests something badly mangled, so the letters of hard and see are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something clings fast, as you can observe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' signals rearranging HARD and SEE together.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling firmly to a surface is to stay fastened to it.
